statement: Scientists should write their papers so that AI tools are more likely to find and cite them.
Hiring and promotion committees should judge scientists by reading a few of their best papers, not by counting papers or citations.
Building shared datasets, software, and tools should count as much as writing papers for jobs and promotion.
The hype about fully autonomous "AI scientists" pulls money and attention away from the basic work science really needs.
Without deliberate action by funders, the benefits of AI in science will go mostly to wealthy universities and countries.
It is fine to have AI write a paper's abstract, as long as the science itself is the scientist's own.
If students can get answers from AI, teachers should spend less time on facts and more on curiosity and thinking skills.
Time a scientist spends following curiosity, with no clear output, should count as real work.
If AI makes it easy to produce papers, the number of papers someone publishes will stop meaning anything.
Students should not use AI that gives direct answers while they are still learning a new skill.
